title: Veteran Journalist Jon Snow Reveals Alzheimer's Diagnosis, Turns His Final Investigation Into a Documentary
summary: For more than three decades, Jon Snow was the trusted face of British television news, guiding viewers through wars, elections, and crises as the lead presenter of Channel 4 News. Now, at 78, he is making headlines himself — by revealing he has Alzheimer's disease. In a candid new documentary, Jon Snow: A Last Big Story, the veteran journalist and his wife, epidemiologist Precious Lunga, let cameras follow them as they navigate his diagnosis. The film, which premieres next week at the Sheffield Documentary Festival, also shows Snow doing what he does best: investigating a major story. This time, it's an environmental disaster in Zambia. "At the beginning I wanted to hide it, there's so much prejudice," Snow says in the film. "Any sort of hint of mental decay, you're sort of dead." But he also emphasizes that the disease is not a constant shadow. "There are moments when it pops up but it's not an all day every day condition, and that's what I cling onto." Alzheimer's, the most common cause of dementia, is often misunderstood. The Alzheimer's Society notes that many people wrongly assume dementia is just a normal part of ageing. Snow's own journey to diagnosis was not straightforward. His wife told the Daily Mail that he was initially reluctant to see a doctor. When he finally did in 2023, he aced a cognitive test — scoring 29 out of 30. It was only a brain scan that confirmed the disease. Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer called Snow "a true giant in journalism" who is now "helping others feel less alone and raising awareness of a condition that affects so many families." Snow himself is pragmatic. "If I don't speak out, who will?" he asked. He even admitted he sometimes doubts the diagnosis. "I mean sometimes I doubt whether I've really got it," he told friend and broadcaster Kirsty Lang. The documentary will air on Channel 4 on June 20. Louisa Compton, Channel 4's head of news, said it was "a profound privilege" to document Snow's last big investigation, framing his journalistic skill alongside a new life lived with Alzheimer's. For a man who spent his career telling other people's stories, this one is deeply personal — and he hopes it will spark change.
why_it_matters: Snow's public disclosure helps challenge the stigma around dementia, showing that a diagnosis does not erase one's abilities or identity, and highlights the importance of brain health awareness among young people.

background_read: Jon Snow anchored Channel 4 News (Britain's flagship evening news programme) for 32 years, covering historic events from the fall of the Berlin Wall to the COVID-19 pandemic, and was known for his impartiality and campaigning on issues like climate change.

Alzheimer's disease (a progressive brain disorder that gradually destroys memory and thinking) is the most common cause of dementia; it is not a normal part of ageing, and its causes involve abnormal protein deposits in the brain.

The Sheffield Documentary Festival (Sheffield Doc/Fest) is a globally respected event in the UK, launched in 1993, that premieres thousands of non-fiction films each year, often sparking social change.

His wife, Dr Precious Lunga (an epidemiologist who studies disease patterns in populations), has worked for UNAIDS and the World Health Organization, using data to tackle infectious diseases like HIV in Africa.
Brain scans like PET can identify amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain, confirming Alzheimer's even when cognitive pen-and-paper tests, like the one Snow aced, do not yet show deficits.

perspectives.description: The documentary raises awareness and reduces stigma, benefitting people with Alzheimer's and their families. Snow's openness shows that life can still hold purpose and meaningful work after a diagnosis, inspiring others to speak out.

Some may argue that exposing his vulnerability could be exploited by the media or that the film oversimplifies a complex disease. There is also concern that a single high-profile case does not address the systemic lack of support for ordinary dementia patients.

The case illustrates how even high-functioning individuals can have Alzheimer's, and how brain scans are crucial for early diagnosis when cognitive tests are inconclusive. It spotlights the intersection between personal story and public health advocacy.

The film could spur more funding for Alzheimer's research or encourage earlier doctor visits. Snow's legacy may shift from journalism to dementia advocacy, potentially influencing public policy on brain health and social care.
